summary: virtualenv: Generated files can follow existing destination links
description:
## Summary

Generated activation files and pyvenv.cfg can follow existing links and write outside the requested environment. The
template writer tests exists() before unlinking, which misses dangling symlinks; the configuration writer opens the
existing path directly.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Final file entries written during environment creation and seeding.

## Attacker-controlled input

Another account must be able to prepare file links in the destination before creation. The invoking user must have write
permission at the linked target. The destination parent must remain controlled during creation; concurrent
parent-directory replacement is a separate concern.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[template writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/via_template.py),
[configuration writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/pyenv_cfg.py).

## Mechanism

`ViaTemplateActivator._generate()` removes an existing output only when `Path.exists()` is true. A dangling symlink
therefore survives, and `write_bytes()` creates its target outside the environment. Other generated files have related
final-entry behavior. `PyEnvCfg.write()` opens `pyvenv.cfg` without first replacing an existing link; a symlink or hard
link there can overwrite an existing target. These paths require a prepared destination tree and the invoking user's
permission to write the linked target.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner's project tree contains `venv/bin/activate -> ../../../.bash_aliases` and an executable `venv/bin/basename`.
Before creation, a new interactive bash does not create the marker. A plain `virtualenv venv` writes the activation
script through the dangling link, creating `~/.bash_aliases` as a regular file. Debian's stock `.bashrc` sources that
file; the next interactive bash adds `venv/bin` to `PATH` and the planted `basename` writes the marker. The reproducer
checks that the link remains, `~/.bash_aliases` appears, and the second shell executes the planted file. A separate
manual check links `pyvenv.cfg` to `~/.bashrc` and observes the latter replaced with generated configuration text.

The link lets creation write outside the requested environment. The attacker chooses the target path but the generated
bytes come from virtualenv. The executable in the example was already in the prepared tree; this finding is not
arbitrary code injection into an otherwise trusted destination. The scanner traces the template behavior to #1454, first
released in 20.0.0b1. [PR #3431](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3431) replaces pre-existing output links and
uses exclusive creation for generated text. It does not make a destination safe if another account can replace parent
directories during creation.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prepared project tree
    participant V as virtualenv writer
    participant H as User home
    participant B as Next interactive bash
    A->>V: venv/bin/activate links to missing ~/.bash_aliases
    V->>V: Path.exists() follows link and returns false
    V->>H: write activation bytes through link
    H-->>B: ~/.bash_aliases now exists
    B->>H: .bashrc sources ~/.bash_aliases
    B->>A: PATH reaches planted venv/bin/basename
    A-->>B: marker created
    Note over V,H: pyvenv.cfg can also overwrite an existing linked target
```

## Reproducer files

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

**`repro`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

# set up: a fresh home with Debian's stock ~/.bashrc, which sources ~/.bash_aliases when that file exists
home = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="home-")
shutil.copy("/etc/skel/.bashrc", f"{home}/.bashrc")
bash_aliases = f"{home}/.bash_aliases"
marker = f"{home}/attacker-ran"
open_terminal = ["bash", "-i", "-c", "true"]
terminal_env = {"HOME": home, "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin", "TERM": "dumb"}

# the attacker's repository, cloned by the user to ~/proj
checkout = f"{home}/proj"
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_hostile_checkout.py", checkout], check=True)
activate = f"{checkout}/venv/bin/activate"
print("shipped: venv/bin/activate ->", os.readlink(activate), flush=True)

# a terminal opened before virtualenv runs does not touch the checkout (stderr: bash -i without a tty warns)
subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)
print("before virtualenv: ~/.bash_aliases exists:", os.path.lexists(bash_aliases), "| marker exists:", os.path.exists(marker), flush=True)
assert not os.path.lexists(bash_aliases) and not os.path.exists(marker)

# trigger: the user creates an environment in the checkout, then opens a new terminal
subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "venv"], cwd=checkout, env={**os.environ, "HOME": home}, check=True)
subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)

# check: the activation script belongs in venv/bin/activate; it must not be written through the link to ~/.bash_aliases
print("venv/bin/activate is still the symlink:", os.path.islink(activate))
written_outside = os.path.isfile(bash_aliases) and not os.path.islink(bash_aliases)
print("~/.bash_aliases created as a regular file:", written_outside)
if written_outside:
    print("  its first line:", open(bash_aliases).readline().rstrip())
attacker_code_ran = os.path.exists(marker)
print("after a new terminal, marker exists:", attacker_code_ran)
if attacker_code_ran:
    print("  it says:", open(marker).read().rstrip())
print("BUG" if written_outside and attacker_code_ran else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/fake_basename.sh`**

```text
#!/bin/sh
echo "attacker code ran as $(id -un)" > "$HOME/attacker-ran"
exec /usr/bin/basename "$@"
```

**`repro.d/make_hostile_checkout.py`**

```text
import os
import shutil
import sys

checkout = sys.argv[1]
bin_dir = os.path.join(checkout, "venv", "bin")
os.makedirs(bin_dir)

# venv/bin/../../.. is the directory holding the checkout, i.e. ~ for a clone at ~/proj; ~/.bash_aliases does not exist
os.symlink("../../../.bash_aliases", os.path.join(bin_dir, "activate"))

# the bash activation script runs $(basename "$VIRTUAL_ENV") right after putting venv/bin first on PATH
fake_basename = os.path.join(bin_dir, "basename")
shutil.copy(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "fake_basename.sh"), fake_basename)
os.chmod(fake_basename, 0o755)
```

## Impact

Creation can overwrite or create files outside the requested environment with the invoking user's permissions. File
contents are constrained by what virtualenv generates.

Severity: medium. CVSS 4.5, `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L`, assigned during maintainer review.

## Versions tested

The confirmed release is 21.14.8. The affected range records that release only; it does not establish the first affected
version or exclude earlier releases. Fixed in 21.14.9.

The fix replaces existing entries, including symbolic and hard links, and exclusively creates generated text
files. Before stdlib creation it replaces executable-directory symlinks and Windows junctions with real directories. It
then removes symbolic and hard links inside that directory, including interpreter executables and DLLs, and at the
configuration and ignore file paths. This also removes unrelated links directly in the executable directory. Final
seed-launcher links are replaced. Exclusive creation protects the final text-file open; delegated stdlib and distlib
writes still require a destination protected from concurrent replacement.

Fix: [PR #3431](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3431).

## Known mitigation

Use a fresh destination beneath an owner-controlled parent. Avoid creation over a tree populated by another account.

## Affected release

- [x] The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8.

## Credits

Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1.

summary: Pillow: Bundled libopenjp2 2.5.4 in all wheels since 11.1.0 carries OSV-2025-219 heap-buffer-overflow write reachable from Image.open().load()
description:
### Summary

Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219

Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.

I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.

Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.

### Details

## Affected wheels

From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:

| Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status |
|---|---|---|
| 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** |
| **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |

Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.

## The defect

`src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:

```c
OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =
    l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =
    l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2;
```

`tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.

The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.

Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.

## Patch status

Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).

The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.

## Suggested remediation

1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file.
2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code.
3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.

## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply

`Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.

I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.

That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.

### Proof of concept

ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:

```
==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 8
    #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086
    #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912
    #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575
    #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793
    #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949
    #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132
located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by
    opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939
```

Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.

I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.

No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.

### Impact

Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.

**Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.

**Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):

```
rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout
rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk
```

Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.

To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

summary: Nuxt: Server-side route rules (`redirect`, `headers`, `proxy`, `ssr`) are skipped for case-variant paths when routing is case-insensitive
description:
## Impact

With the default `router.options.sensitive: false`, Nuxt's page router resolves routes case-insensitively, so `/Admin` renders the same page as `/admin`. On the server, however, route rules were resolved with Nitro's route-rule matcher, which matches keys case-sensitively. A request whose path differs from a rule key only in letter case therefore rendered the page with none of that rule applied.

Earlier fixes ([GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47), [GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9)) case-folded the route rules that the Nuxt app itself reads, such as `appMiddleware`. This advisory covers the rules applied on the server:

- `redirect`: a rule used to send visitors away from a page, such as `'/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' }`, was skipped, and the page and its server-fetched data were rendered instead.
- `headers`: per-route response headers, including security headers such as `Content-Security-Policy` or `X-Frame-Options`, were not sent.
- `proxy`: the request was not proxied.
- `ssr: false` and `noScripts`: the page was server-rendered, or shipped scripts, despite the rule.
- `getRouteRules(event)` (auto-imported, or from `nuxt/server`) and `matchRouteRules` from `nuxt/server` returned no rules for the case variant.

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' },
  },
})
```

With this configuration, `/admin/secret` redirects to `/login`, but `/Admin/secret` rendered `app/pages/admin/secret.vue`.

## Mitigating factors

- Applications that set `router.options.sensitive: true` in `nuxt.config` are not affected, because their pages are only served for the exact case of the route.
- Access checks performed in server middleware, route middleware attached with `definePageMeta`, or in the page's data fetching are not affected. The issue only affects protections that rely on a server-side route rule matching the request path.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `<4.6.2`, including all Nuxt 3 releases, and `@nuxt/nitro-server` `<4.6.2`.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.2`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Nuxt now resolves server-side route rules itself, decoding and case-folding both the rule keys and the request path unless `router.options.sensitive` is set, and applies the result to Nitro's `redirect`, `headers` and `proxy` handling, the renderer, and the `getRouteRules` / `matchRouteRules` helpers.

When routing is case-insensitive, patched releases change some behaviour:

- Route rules also apply to case variants of server API routes. For example, `/API/x` now matches a `/api/**` `proxy` or `headers` rule.
- Rule keys that differ only in letter case now resolve to the same path on the server, and the later key takes precedence.

The following are not changed by this fix:

- `cache` and `swr` response caching is attached to server routes by Nitro's router, which matches case-sensitively. A case variant is still rendered with its route rules applied, but its response is not cached.
- Rules that a deployment preset compiles into platform configuration (for example Vercel's `config.json` or Netlify's `_redirects` and `_headers`) are matched by the platform. Once a request reaches the Nuxt server, the rules are applied as described above.
- If `sensitive` is set only in `app/router.options.ts`, the server follows the `nuxt.config` value. In that configuration route rules can only apply to more paths, never fewer.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.2`. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

1. Set `router: { options: { sensitive: true } }` in `nuxt.config`, so pages are only served for the exact case of their route.
2. Alternatively, enforce access control in server middleware or route middleware rather than relying on a `redirect` route rule, and set security headers for every response rather than per route.

summary: Nuxt server islands render `useHeadSafe` input without sanitisation
description:
## Impact

`useHeadSafe` restricts head input to an allowlist of safe tags and attributes. For example, `bodyAttrs` is limited to `class` and `style`, event handler attributes are removed, and `<script>` tags are only kept for JSON types.

When `useHeadSafe` is called inside a server island (a `.server.vue` component or page, or a component rendered with `<NuxtIsland>`), the island renderer serialises the raw input of every head entry into the island response without the option that marks it as safe input. `<NuxtIsland>` then pushes that input into the page's head as a regular entry, both during server rendering and when hydrating or refetching on the client.

As a result, input that `useHeadSafe` would normally strip (such as `bodyAttrs.onload` or executable `<script>` content) is rendered into the page. If an application passes user-controlled data to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island, an attacker who controls that data can achieve stored cross-site scripting on the application's origin.

```vue
<!-- components/AuthorMeta.server.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
const { data: author } = await useFetch('/api/author')
// author.value.head is user-authored, e.g. { bodyAttrs: { onload: '...' } }
useHeadSafe(author.value.head)
</script>
```

## Mitigating factors

- Server components are experimental. They are only active when the application defines a `.server.vue` component or page, or enables `experimental.componentIslands` and renders `<NuxtIsland>`.
- Exploitation requires the application to pass attacker-controlled data to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island. `useHeadSafe` called from regular (non-island) components and pages is not affected.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `>=3.13.0`, when head support for server islands was introduced. Nuxt 2 is not affected.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.2`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Patched releases apply Unhead's safe input filtering to `useHeadSafe` entries on the server before they are added to the island response, so `islandResponse.head` (including what `render:island` hooks see) only contains input that `useHeadSafe` allows.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.2`. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

1. Call `useHeadSafe` with untrusted input from a regular component or page rather than from inside a server island.
2. Alternatively, validate untrusted head input against your own allowlist before passing it to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island.

summary: Nuxt: Incomplete fix for GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26: a `javascript:` URL prefixed with an ASCII control character executes from `<NuxtLink>` when `pages` is disabled
description:
## Impact

An application that renders `<NuxtLink :to="...">` with a value it does not control can be made to render an anchor whose `href` executes script in the application's origin when clicked.

This is an incomplete fix for [GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26) (CVE-2026-53722). It only affects applications running without a `pages/` directory, where `pages` resolves to `false` and Nuxt registers its own router in place of vue-router. Applications using vue-router are not affected.

Prefixing `javascript:` with an ASCII C0 control character, for example `%01`, meant the value was not recognised as having a protocol. It was classified as an internal route and so never reached the protocol check added in GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26, and the router used for `pages: false` passed it through to the rendered `href` unchanged. Browsers strip the leading control character and run the result as a script URL.

Both `<NuxtLink custom>` and the default anchor are affected, and the `href` is present in the server-rendered HTML.

## Mitigating factors

- The application must have `pages` disabled (no `pages/` directory, or `pages: false`).
- The application must bind untrusted input to `:to`.
- A victim must click the rendered link.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `<4.6.0`, including all Nuxt 3 releases. Versions before `4.4.7` and `3.21.7` are also affected by GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.0`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Anchor `href` values are now checked for script-capable protocols wherever they are rendered, including the router used when `pages` is disabled. Protocol detection also moved to the platform `URL` parser, so a URL is classified the same way the browser will read it.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.0` or later. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3, validate values before binding them to `:to`, for example by rejecting anything that is not a path beginning with a single `/`.

summary: Nuxt: Route rules are matched against the raw request path, so a percent-encoded segment can bypass `appMiddleware` on dynamic and catch-all routes
description:
### Summary

Nuxt compared `routeRules` keys against the raw request path, without decoding percent-encoding, while the router decodes parameters when it resolves a route. A request whose path is percent-encoded can therefore resolve to a page while failing to match the route rule meant to protect it, so the rule's `appMiddleware` never runs, including during server rendering.

### Impact

For a page served through a dynamic or catch-all route, an attacker can percent-encode a character in the path to skip the rule:

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/users/admin': { appMiddleware: 'auth' },
  },
})
```

Requesting `/users/%61dmin` still renders `app/pages/users/[id].vue` with `id` decoded to `admin`, but the rule keyed `/users/admin` does not match, so `auth` does not run and the server renders and returns the gated page to an unauthenticated visitor. No privileges and no user interaction are required, and only ASCII characters are involved.

Purely static ASCII routes are not affected: static segments are matched without decoding, so a request for `/%61dmin` does not resolve to the page registered at `/admin` and 404s instead of rendering.

The rule keys affected are the ones carried in the app manifest and consumed by the app: `appMiddleware`, `redirect`, `appLayout`, `ssr`, `prerender`, and the payload flags derived from `cache`, `isr` and `swr`.

If you have pinned or overridden dependency versions below what your Nuxt release declares, a release outside the affected ranges can still be exposed, so do not conclude from a single reproduction that you are unaffected.

### Patches

Releases from `4.4.4` and `3.21.4` are not affected, because their dependency floor requires a version of the underlying HTTP layer that normalises percent-encoding in the request path before routing, which removes the mismatch in a default install.

The comparison itself is fixed in `nuxt@4.5.2` and `nuxt@3.21.11`: route-rule keys and lookup paths are now decoded (and, unless `router.options.sensitive` is set, case-folded) before they are compared. Reserved escapes such as `%2F` are left encoded, so decoding cannot introduce extra path segments, and paths that cannot be decoded are matched verbatim. Upgrading to those releases is recommended, since it fixes the comparison rather than relying on a dependency to normalise the input, and it also restores route rules for pages whose paths contain non-ASCII characters.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not rely on a `routeRules` key alone to protect a route. Attach the middleware to the page itself, which binds it to the resolved route rather than to the raw path string:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
definePageMeta({ middleware: 'auth' })
</script>
```

### Credits

Thanks to @sushi-gif, whose report that route rules keyed with non-ASCII paths never match the routes generated for those pages prompted the review that found this issue.

summary: pypdf: Possible long runtimes/large memory usage when retrieving form fields
description:
### Impact

An attacker who uses this vulnerability can craft a PDF which leads to large memory usage and/or long runtimes. This requires retrieving the form fields of a document.

### Patches

This has been fixed in [pypdf==6.21.0](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/releases/tag/6.21.0).

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, consider applying the changes from PR [#4219](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/pull/4219).

summary: pypdf: Possible large memory usage when parsing arrays and dictionaries
description:
### Impact

An attacker who uses this vulnerability can craft a PDF which leads to large memory usage. This requires parsing arrays and/or dictionaries with lots of elements.

### Patches

This has been fixed in [pypdf==6.21.0](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/releases/tag/6.21.0).

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, consider applying the changes from PR [#4218](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/pull/4218).

summary: Electron: SameSite cookie restrictions are not applied to windows opened from links
description:
### Impact

Pages opened into a new window from a link were loaded as if the app itself had navigated there rather than the page that contained the link, so the request was treated as same-site: `SameSite=Strict` cookies were sent and `Sec-Fetch-Site` did not identify the initiating page. Content shown in the app could use this to make a credentialed top-level request to another site that relies on SameSite cookies as a CSRF defence.

Apps are only affected if they load untrusted content and allow it to open new windows. Apps that deny new windows from untrusted content with `setWindowOpenHandler` are not affected.

### Workarounds

Return `{ action: 'deny' }` from `setWindowOpenHandler` for windows opened by untrusted content.

### Fixed Versions

* `45.0.0-alpha.6`
* `44.3.0`
* `43.7.0`
* `42.11.3`

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)
